Affirming
uh-FUR-ming
adjective / participle
From Latin affirmare, to make firm, to assert as true. To affirm is to confirm, to declare true, to uphold. In recent church usage 'affirming' has become a near-technical litmus term: to be 'affirming' is to endorse same-sex relationships and transgender identity as good, blessed, and beyond repentance — the word for whether a church or person will bless what God calls sin.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
A litmus for blessing what God calls sin; love affirms the sinner's worth and God's truth, but never the sin.

📖 Biblical Definition

Genuine biblical love does affirm much about a person: that he is made in the image of God (Gen. 1:27), of immeasurable worth, and the object of a love that 'commendeth' itself toward sinners (Rom. 5:8). But love never affirms sin, because love 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' (1 Cor. 13:6). The same love that 'speaks the truth' does so 'in love' (Eph. 4:15), and the love of Christ for His own is explicitly a rebuking, correcting love: 'As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent' (Rev. 3:19). To love is to will another's true good, which can never include confirming him in what damns him. The biblical pattern is the woman at the well and the woman taken in adultery: full personal welcome joined to 'go, and sin no more' (John 8:11). Scripture affirms the sinner's worth and the truth of God; it will not affirm the sin.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The litmus term for endorsing what God calls sin; but biblical love affirms a person's God-given worth while refusing to bless his sin, for love rejoices in the truth and rebukes those it loves (Rev. 3:19).

AFFIRMING, adjective. To confirm or declare good; in current church usage, to endorse same-sex relationships and transgender identity as blessed and requiring no repentance.

From Latin affirmare, to make firm, to assert as true.

True affirmation: love confirms a person's worth as God's image-bearer (Gen. 1:27) and the truth of God's Word (1 Cor. 13:6).

Corrupt use: 'affirming' as a banner for blessing sin — against Eph. 4:15 (truth in love) and Rev. 3:19 (Christ rebukes those He loves).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 13:6 — "Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth;"

Ephesians 4:15 — "But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:"

Revelation 3:19 — "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent."

Romans 1:32 — "Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them."

John 8:11 — "She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."

Leviticus 19:17 — "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A good word for confirming what is true is bent into a banner for blessing what God forbids, so that to refuse the blessing is recast as a failure to love; but love rejoices in the truth and rebukes those it loves.

expand to see more

The corruption hangs on a false definition of love. 'Affirming' assumes that to love a person is to confirm whatever he desires and to call good whatever he calls good, so that any refusal to bless his sin is, by definition, a withholding of love. But Scripture defines love otherwise: love 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' (1 Cor. 13:6), and a love that rejoices in what God condemns has already ceased to be the love Scripture commends. The most pointed text is Romans 1:32, which names as the bottom of the descent not merely doing what God forbids but 'have pleasure in them that do them' — affirmation of the sin of others. The very posture the word 'affirming' prizes is the one Paul names as the depth of the fall.

The move also misreads the love of Christ, which is everywhere a correcting love. 'As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent' (Rev. 3:19) — rebuke is not the opposite of His love but its expression. The law itself binds love to correction: 'thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him' (Lev. 19:17); to leave a brother in his sin without a word is there named a species of hatred, not love. So the affirming church, congratulating itself on its compassion, is in fact withholding the one thing love is bound to give: the truth that calls a soul to repentance and life. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the affirming program of blessing same-sex and transgender identity is named here to rebut it.

The recovery is to hold the two affirmations Scripture actually makes — and to refuse the one it forbids. The believer affirms, without reserve, the worth of every person as God's image-bearer (Gen. 1:27), and welcomes the sinner as Christ welcomed sinners, with nothing held back of personal love. He affirms, just as firmly, the truth of God's Word about sin and salvation. What he will not do is affirm the sin, for that would be to hate the sinner under the costume of love, confirming him in the very thing that will destroy him. 'Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more' (John 8:11) is the pattern: full welcome, no condemnation of the person — and no blessing of the sin.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin affirmare, to make firm, to declare true; now a litmus for blessing sin. Love affirms the sinner's worth and God's truth, never the sin, and rebukes those it loves (Rev. 3:19).

expand to see more

Latin: affirmare, to make firm, to assert as true — to confirm or uphold.

Biblical love: 1 Cor. 13:6, love 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' — the boundary the litmus crosses.

Correcting love: Rev. 3:19 and Lev. 19:17 — Christ rebukes whom He loves; to leave sin unrebuked is hatred, not affirmation.

Usage

"They called the church 'affirming' for blessing the sin, but love rejoices in the truth, not in iniquity."

"Romans 1 names taking pleasure in the sin of others as the bottom of the fall — the very thing 'affirming' prizes as compassion."

"Christ said 'neither do I condemn thee' and 'go, and sin no more' in one breath; that is affirmation of the person and refusal of the sin."
